flipKeys' own trailing `sortKeys(trackFor(g.holder, g.prop))` call (motion.js:11674) is NOT merely defensive symmetry with distributeKeys — it is functionally required. Traced by hand on a 3-key example with frames [10,20,30]: `slots = [10,20,30].reverse() = [30,20,10]`; the forEach then assigns rank0(originally frame 10) → 30, rank1(originally frame 20) → 20, rank2(originally frame 30) → 10 — the resulting `track.keys` ARRAY order (unchanged, still rank0/1/2) now holds frames [30,20,10], descending, no longer matching frame-ascending order. Without the sortKeys call immediately after, every OTHER reader of `track.keys` that assumes frame-ascending order (segmentLeftKey, C20n; the timeline row renderers, C20h/C20i) would misbehave on a freshly-flipped track until some unrelated write happened to re-sort it.

packets.responsibility: layerIndexOfHolder(holder) (11434-11444, lead-in 11431-11433): returns `state.layers.indexOf(holder)` directly if `holder` IS a layer object (owns its own tracks); otherwise scans every layer's own `elementMotion` dict values (`for (var k in em)`, own-property guarded) for an identity match, returning the OWNING layer's index; -1 if not found anywhere. Pure input->output, and uniform across element/mesh/text-animator holders because all three live in the SAME `ld.elementMotion[id]` dict regardless of whether `id` is a shape's strokeId, a mesh vertex-group's meshId, or a text-animator character's strokeId (CLAUDE.md §12ter point 1; construction site motion.js:2881-2897, C20n, sibling-covered) — this function performs no id-kind-specific branching of its own. syncLayerSelToKeySel() (11451-11472, lead-in 11445-11450 citing feedback #791): guarded no-op outside Motion mode (`state.appMode !== 'motion'`) and during an active marquee drag (`if (_motionMarquee) return`, a genuine forward reference to a global declared later at motion.js:11925, C20q — see boundaries); early-returns if `_motionKeySel` is empty (comment: clearing a key selection never clears layers).
